question: On 26 February 2025, the Commission presented the Clean Industrial Deal, which is meant to result in lower energy prices and the creation of quality jobs. Investment in Europe’s chemicals sector fell by over 80 % in 2025 and plant closures doubled. There is a real danger that the continent will become dependent on China for the raw materials needed for the automotive, health and defence industries.

The sector is struggling with high energy prices, suffocating bureaucracy and the growth in Chinese imports. Announcements of plant closures have impacted directly on around 20 000 jobs across Europe since 2022 and last year wiped out 17.2 megatonnes in production capacity. I would therefore like to put the following questions to the Commission: 1.
Given the measures taken by the Commission, how will it guarantee a genuine reduction in energy bills, and that energy costs are not simply redistributed?
Are decarbonisation plans not over-ambitious and unrealistic given the increase in global demand for cheap and secure energy?
Is the Commission prepared to reform the Clean Industrial Deal it presented, and in particular to abolish carbon quotas?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.6.2026) The EU internal electricity market delivers annually EUR 34 billion of benefits. The completion of the internal energy market could additionally deliver up to EUR 40 billion by 2030 and will be instrumental to further strengthen energy security and achieve the decarbonisation goals while at the same time decreasing price volatility and ensuring affordability.

The Commission is currently in full swing implementing the Clean Industrial Deal1 (CID), with many initiatives already published, such as the Affordable Energy Action Plan2, the Clean Industrial Deal State aid framework3, the strengthening of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, the adoption of the Commission proposal for an Industrial Accelerator Act4.

In light of the Middle East conflict, the Commission also published the AccelerateEU plan5 to strengthen EU energy resilience and adopted the Middle East Temporary State Aid Framework6. These initiatives combine a series of measures aimed at delivering a reduction in energy bills through the deployment of home-grown clean electricity and the transition of industries towards more efficient energy vectors.

In parallel, to shield industrial consumers from high prices in the short term, targeted measures, including a legislative proposal on network charges and taxation will be proposed to mitigate the impact of high electricity prices compared to those of competitors.

To further implement the CID, more initiatives will be launched in 2026, such as the Circular Economy Act, legislative proposal to revise the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) creating an Industrial Decarbonisation Bank to support decarbonisation investments in energyintensive industries.
